tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

+/* *******************************************************************************************************************
+ * Application: ClaudeCodeExtension
+ *
+ * Autor:  Daniel Carvalho Liedke / Claude Code
+ *
+ * Copyright © Daniel Carvalho Liedke 2026
+ * Usage and reproduction in any manner whatsoever without the written permission of Daniel Carvalho Liedke is strictly forbidden.
+ *
+ * Purpose: Overflow rule for the ◀/▶ scroll arrows of the panel toolbar and the composer action row
+ *
+ * *******************************************************************************************************************/
+
+using System.Windows;
+
+namespace ClaudeCodeVS.UI
+{
+    /// <summary>
+    /// Decides whether a scrolled toolbar row needs its ◀/▶ arrows. The arrows take their room from
+    /// the scroller itself, so reading the scroller's own viewport would count them against the
+    /// content: once shown they kept themselves shown until the row was widened by their width, and a
+    /// row first laid out narrow (VS start, a new chat tab) kept them for good. The rule is unit-tested
+    /// in <c>Tests/ScrollArrowsTests.cs</c>.
+    /// </summary>
+    public static class ScrollArrows
+    {
+        /// <summary>
+        /// True when the content overflows the room the row would have with no arrows at all:
+        /// <paramref name="viewport"/> plus the width the currently shown arrows take
+        /// (<paramref name="shownArrowsWidth"/>, margins included).
+        /// </summary>
+        public static bool ContentOverflows(double extent, double viewport, double shownArrowsWidth)
+        {
+            return extent > viewport + shownArrowsWidth + 0.5;
+        }
+
+        /// <summary>Width an arrow currently takes from its row, margins included; 0 while collapsed.</summary>
+        public static double ShownWidth(FrameworkElement arrow)
+        {
+            return arrow.Visibility == Visibility.Visible
+                ? arrow.ActualWidth + arrow.Margin.Left + arrow.Margin.Right
+                : 0;
+        }
+    }
+}
diff --git a/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md b/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md
index d212fce..ab1aeb4 100644
--- a/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md
+++ b/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md
@@ -142,6 +142,7 @@ Why it exists (v191.0): the embedded terminal is a window of another process (WT
 - Round 9 (still v170.0): two reports that the round 7/8 fixes hadn't fully landed. (1) Native mode still showed a dead vertical strip between the panel's title bar and the usage bars once the chat owned its own tab. `RefreshToolbarLayout()`'s `IsChatDetachedToOwnTab` branch collapses every *control* in that area, but two containers kept reserving height regardless: `ControlsRow` holds the ◀/▶ scroll arrows, which are deliberately `Visibility.Hidden` rather than `Collapsed` (so the toolbar's footprint doesn't jump as they come and go — see round 6), and `CheckboxRow`'s empty file-chips row still contributed its own margins. With the prompt box also auto-hidden in that state (Change B), the usage bars are the only thing the panel still owns, so the reserved height read as pure wasted space. Fixed by collapsing the two rows themselves — `Visibility panelRows = IsChatDetachedToOwnTab ? Visibility.Collapsed : Visibility.Visible;` applied to `ControlsRow` and `CheckboxRow` — which also makes the individual control collapses redundant-but-harmless and restores both rows the moment the chat docks back. (2) In classic terminal mode the ◀/▶ arrows never appeared and the row never scrolled, with ⚙ still arranged past the tool window's visible right edge. Round 7's Auto→Star fix on `ControlsRow` and round 8's `HorizontalAlignment="Right"` on the scroller were both treating symptoms of the wrong layout primitive: `RightButtonsRow` was a Grid whose columns split the available width *proportionally*, independent of what each child actually needs, so the scroller was handed a viewport wider than the panel (nothing to scroll ⇒ `ScrollableWidth == 0` ⇒ arrows stay Hidden forever) while the fixed group's column started past the visible edge. Replaced the Grid with a `DockPanel` (`LastChildFill="True"`): ◀ docks Left, then `FixedRightButtonsPanel` and ▶ dock Right (fixed group first in document order so it ends up rightmost, ▶ immediately to its left), and `RightButtonsScroller` is the last child. A DockPanel measures each docked child against the space *genuinely remaining* and gives the fill child exactly the leftover, so the fixed group can never be arranged outside the panel and the scroller's viewport is always the real available width — which is what makes `ScrollableWidth` become positive and the arrows show up. The scroller keeps round 8's `HorizontalAlignment="Right"` so slack when everything fits lands on its own left edge rather than between the promoted buttons and the fixed group. `RightButtonsScroller_ScrollChanged` also changed: it used to hide whichever arrow had nowhere left to go, so the row typically displayed a single lone arrow, which reads as decoration rather than as "there's more over here" — the reporter didn't recognize the row as scrollable at all. Now both arrows become `Visible` together as soon as `ScrollableWidth > 0.5`, with `IsEnabled` reflecting each direction so the exhausted end greys out instead of vanishing; `Hidden` (never `Collapsed`) is still the not-scrollable state, since the arrows are docked and a `Collapsed` one would give its slice back and shift the whole row.
 - Round 10 (still v170.0): the reporter switched back to classic terminal mode and the `⚙` Settings/Agent button was simply gone from the panel's toolbar — the row ended at `🤖`, with no `⚙` past it and no `📎` in the left cluster either. Not a layout overflow (the DockPanel from round 9 was bounding the row correctly, which is why the ◀/▶ arrows were working in that same screenshot): `MenuDropdownButton.Visibility` is assigned in exactly *one* place in the whole codebase — the `if (IsChatDetachedToOwnTab)` block in `RefreshToolbarLayout()` — and that assignment only ever sets `Collapsed`. Every other control that block collapses is recomputed from scratch earlier in the same method and therefore heals on the next pass (the `Apply(...)` loop rebuilds the nine feature buttons and their menu items, `hasConsole && hasModelMenu` rebuilds `🤖`, `anyInDropdown` rebuilds `☰`), so the asymmetry went unnoticed; `⚙`, `📎` `AttachDropdownButton`, `▶` `SendPromptButton` and `⚡` `CustomCommandsButton` have no such authority. Once the chat had been detached to its own tab even briefly, those four were collapsed for good — turning native mode off dropped straight past the branch with nothing restoring them, and `⚙` in particular has no fallback anywhere (it is not part of the customizable toolbar, so it can't be re-promoted, and the Settings dialog is only reachable through it). Fixed by giving the branch an `else` that restores each one *by its own rule* rather than forcing `Visible`: `⚙` and `📎` unconditionally visible (they have no other gate), `▶` per `_settings.SendWithEnter`, and `⚡` by simply calling `RefreshCustomCommandsButton()` — the actual authority, which already handles both the empty-command-list case and the round-8 `!IsChatDetachedToOwnTab` gate, and does not call back into `RefreshToolbarLayout()`. General rule this leaves behind: any control collapsed inside a state-specific branch of `RefreshToolbarLayout()` needs a matching restore in the other branch unless something unconditional in the method already recomputes it.
 - Round 11: a fresh native-mode screenshot showed a large gap between the fixed selectors (ending in "Ask permission ▾") and the first mirrored icon button. Cause: `ComposerActionsScroller` had been given round 8's `HorizontalAlignment="Right"` fix verbatim, but `ComposerActionRow`'s layout is the mirror image of `RightButtonsRow`'s — the fixed group sits in column 0, to the scroller's *left*, not docked to its right like `RightButtonsRow`'s `FixedRightButtonsPanel`. Right-aligning shrank the scroller to its content's width and pinned it to column 2's right edge, pushing all the Star column's slack into the gap on its left, right where the mirrored buttons should have started. Fixed by changing it to `HorizontalAlignment="Left"`, which pins the scroller flush against the fixed group when everything fits and still expands to the full available width (no alignment effect) once content overflows and needs to scroll. Same screenshot also showed dead space below the action row before the input box: `ComposerActionRow`'s bottom margin (6px) plus the empty attachment-chip `WrapPanel`'s own bottom margin (4px) added up regardless of whether there were any chips to show. Trimmed the action row's margin to 4px and moved the chip strip's margin into code (`UpdateSessionAttachmentChips`/`UpdateComposerAttachmentChips` in `ClaudeCodeControl.NativeChat.cs` now set `host.Margin` to 4px only when `Children.Count > 0`, 0 otherwise) so an empty strip stops reserving space it isn't using.
+- Arrow overflow rule (v304.0): `RightButtonsScroller_ScrollChanged` and `ComposerActionsScroller_ScrollChanged` decide overflow with `ScrollArrows.ContentOverflows(extent, viewport, shownArrowsWidth)` — the viewport plus the width (margins included) of the arrows currently shown, i.e. the room the row would have with no arrows. Reading `ScrollableWidth` counted the arrows' own slots against the content: once shown they stayed until the row was widened by their width (dragging the edge back and forth to find the size), and a row first laid out narrow (VS start, a new chat tab) kept them at full width. Hiding them re-runs layout with a wider viewport, so the decision is stable both ways.
 - Round 12: a follow-up screenshot, now with the row 11 fixes applied and the window narrow enough to trigger scrolling, showed a gap next to the ◀ arrow. Cause: round 5's choice of `Visibility.Hidden` over `Collapsed` for the arrow buttons — made for the *classic* toolbar's `RightButtonsRow`, where an `Auto` column collapsing really would shift a `DockPanel`'s docked children — was reused here even though `ComposerActionRow`'s arrow columns are also `Auto` but sit next to the row's only Star column (`ComposerActionsScroller`), which is itself bounded by `ComposerBar`'s fixed width. +/* *******************************************************************************************************************
+ * Application: ClaudeCodeExtension
+ *
+ * Autor:  Daniel Carvalho Liedke / Claude Code
+ *
+ * Copyright © Daniel Carvalho Liedke 2026
+ * Usage and reproduction in any manner whatsoever without the written permission of Daniel Carvalho Liedke is strictly forbidden.
+ *
+ * Purpose: Overflow rule for the ◀/▶ scroll arrows of the panel toolbar and the composer action row
+ *
+ * *******************************************************************************************************************/
+
+using System.Windows;
+
+namespace ClaudeCodeVS.UI
+{
+    /// <summary>
+    /// Decides whether a scrolled toolbar row needs its ◀/▶ arrows. The arrows take their room from
+    /// the scroller itself, so reading the scroller's own viewport would count them against the
+    /// content: once shown they kept themselves shown until the row was widened by their width, and a
+    /// row first laid out narrow (VS start, a new chat tab) kept them for good. The rule is unit-tested
+    /// in <c>Tests/ScrollArrowsTests.cs</c>.
+    /// </summary>
+    public static class ScrollArrows
+    {
+        /// <summary>
+        /// True when the content overflows the room the row would have with no arrows at all:
+        /// <paramref name="viewport"/> plus the width the currently shown arrows take
+        /// (<paramref name="shownArrowsWidth"/>, margins included).
+        /// </summary>
+        public static bool ContentOverflows(double extent, double viewport, double shownArrowsWidth)
+        {
+            return extent > viewport + shownArrowsWidth + 0.5;
+        }
+
+        /// <summary>Width an arrow currently takes from its row, margins included; 0 while collapsed.</summary>
+        public static double ShownWidth(FrameworkElement arrow)
+        {
+            return arrow.Visibility == Visibility.Visible
+                ? arrow.ActualWidth + arrow.Margin.Left + arrow.Margin.Right
+                : 0;
+        }
+    }
+}

217-- The usage popup in the chat composer shows the e-mail of the claude.ai account the limits belong to.

### Version 304.0
